hops.afterHeading: How small is too small to see?
hops.title: A paper microscope that survives a stomp
hops.text: Fold some pre-cut paper parts for under ten minutes, add a tiny round lens, and you have a working microscope. Stanford researchers described this Foldscope in 2014. Bought in bulk, its parts cost less than a dollar, and it weighs less than two nickels. With a 1,450-times lens, it showed stained blood cells and bacteria. Its makers say it even survives a three-story drop or a stomp.

sources.citation: Cybulski JS, Clements J, Prakash M (2014). Foldscope: Origami-Based Paper Microscope. PLOS ONE 9(6): e98781.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A child lying on a wooden floor watches a sneaker step down beside a small folded paper microscope with a tiny round lens.
image.caption: Bought in bulk, a paper microscope's parts cost under a dollar, and its one tiny lens shows cells.

hops.title: Pasteur's swan-neck flasks
hops.text: In the 1850s, many people still thought microbes popped out of clear broth all on their own. Louis Pasteur tested that by boiling broth in glass flasks with long, curving swan necks open to the air. Microbes from the air got stuck in the bend, so the broth stayed clear. Then he broke off a neck, and microbes soon grew. His experiments won a prize in 1862.

sources.citation: Parker N, Schneegurt M, Thi Tu A-H, Lister P, Forster BM (2016). Microbiology, Section 3.1: Spontaneous Generation. OpenStax.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two glass flasks on a wooden bench, one with a long curved neck and clear broth, one with a broken neck and cloudy broth.
image.caption: The curved neck trapped microbes from the air; once Pasteur broke it off, microbes grew.

hops.title: Electron microscope pictures start out gray
hops.text: Science posters are full of purple bacteria and neon-green pollen, so it is easy to think tiny things look that bright. A scanning electron microscope actually works in the dark, using a beam of electrons instead of light. It records only how strong the signal is at each spot, so its raw picture comes out in shades of gray. People add the colors afterward so the parts stand out.

sources.citation: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Small Wonders.

Parker N, Schneegurt M, Thi Tu A-H, Lister P, Forster BM (2016). Microbiology, Section 2.3: Instruments of Microscopy. OpenStax; Pirozzi NM, Hoogenboom JP, Giepmans BNG (2018). Histochemistry and Cell Biology 150: 509–520.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A smiling spiky pollen grain, half gray and half being painted teal, green and gold by a person with a small paintbrush.
image.caption: Electron microscope pictures start out gray; the bright colors are added afterward.

audio.title: Kingdoms on your teeth, an overnight dye mistake, and a one-celled wineglass
audio.transcript:
You probably trust your own eyes. Look at a glass of clear water or a clean tooth, and it seems obvious what is there and what is not. Here are three true stories about how sneaky the world of cells can be.

First, check your own mouth. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek did not stop at looking at rainwater. In sixteen eighty-three, he wrote a letter to the Royal Society of London about the white plaque on teeth. Under his tiny single-lens microscope, he saw crowds of little living things moving wildly around. He wrote that there were so many of them on a person's teeth that he believed they outnumbered the people in a whole kingdom. As wild as that sounded, he guessed low. One scientific review estimates that an average healthy person carries nearly as many bacteria on their teeth as there are people on Earth. And every day, you swallow an average of eighty billion bacteria in your saliva. Each one is far smaller than the eye line of about one hundred micrometres, so you never see them one by one.

Second, even when a microscope magnifies a cell past the eye line, cells pull another trick: many of them are nearly clear, so they blend into the background. In eighteen fifty-eight, a German researcher named Joseph von Gerlach was working at the University of Erlangen. He was trying to make details in brain tissue easier to see with a red dye called carmine. By mistake, he left a piece of tissue soaking in the dye overnight. The next morning, the extra soaking had stained the brain cells far more clearly than before. The lesson from that lucky mistake: a stain can make nearly clear cells stand out.

Third, once you learn that most cells are too small to see, it is easy to guess that anything big must be made of many cells, and anything tiny must be just one. Living things love breaking both guesses. In the sea lives a green alga nicknamed the mermaid's wineglass. When fully grown, it stands about three centimetres tall. That is thirty times the width of the frog egg at the top of your size table. You can see it without a microscope, and yet the whole alga is one single giant cell. Now flip the rule. A water bear, also called a tardigrade, is usually less than one millimetre long, so you need a microscope to see it well. Even so, a water bear is a full animal built from about one thousand cells. Some of its tiny muscles are each made of just one cell.

Put those three stories together and you get the reason microscopes changed biology. Invisible does not mean empty. Big does not always mean many cells. And tiny does not always mean just one cell. You only find out by looking closely.
